<explanation>
Based on the provided file tree and README, this project is Fider—a self-hosted feedback portal that enables organizations to collect feature requests and suggestions from their users. It’s a full-stack application built primarily in Go (for the backend/core services) with a modern JavaScript/TypeScript frontend (using React components placed under the public directory). The project integrates multiple external services (billing via Paddle, various email providers like AWS SES, Mailgun, SMTP, etc.) and has a well‐structured codebase that makes use of different architectural layers.

Below is a step-by-step guide on how to draw a detailed system design diagram for Fider:

1. Identify the Main Components
   • Frontend Client: Represented by the “public” folder which holds the React components, pages, hooks, models, and service-related code. This layer handles the user interface (UI) and client-side logic, including server-side rendering (indicated by files such as ssr.tsx).
   • Backend API & Business Logic: The “app” directory contains the core backend logic. This includes:
     – Actions: Contains business logic for various operations (user management, posts, tags, billing, invites, OAuth, etc.).
     – Handlers: HTTP API endpoints. You have both generic endpoints and versioned API handlers (apiv1).
     – Middlewares: Components that provide cross-cutting concerns such as authentication, caching, CORS, instrumentation, and security.
     – Models & Data Layer: Organized under “models”, this layer defines the database entities, DTOs (data transfer objects), and query layers. There’s also an extraction to “services/sqlstore” for interacting with the underlying database, likely PostgreSQL as hinted by the SQL migration scripts under “migrations” and package names ("postgres").
     – Jobs & Tasks: Background jobs and asynchronous tasks (e.g., email suppression, purge of notifications).
     – Services & External Integrations: Provided under “services” and “pkg” directories, this includes integrations for email, billing (Paddle), blob storage (local file system, S3, SQL blob), HTTP clients, logging, JWT authentication, and more.
   • Database: While the project does not explicitly include a database folder, migration SQL files under “migrations” indicate the schema creation and updates. In your diagram, a “Database” component (like PostgreSQL) should be included to show where persistent data is stored.
   • External Services: There are integrations with third-party providers:
     – Billing providers (e.g., Paddle)
     – Email services (AWS SES, Mailgun, SMTP, plus a mock implementation)
     – OAuth providers, webhooks, etc.
   • DevOps/Deployment: The presence of Dockerfile, docker-compose.yml, and Kubernetes/Procfile (for Heroku or similar) shows containerization and process management. Also, configuration-related files like .env, Makefile, and GitHub workflows indicate CI/CD pipelines.

2. Define Relationships and Data Flows
   • The Frontend communicates with the Backend via HTTP/REST API calls (or SSR calls). Represent the flow from the “public” UI components to the “handlers” in the backend.
   • The Handlers, using the “actions” layer and “middlewares”, process HTTP requests, interact with the “models” (and hence the Database), and integrate with external services (billing, email).
   • The background “jobs” and “tasks” run asynchronously to perform time-based or event-driven operations.
   • External integrations (such as email or billing) are invoked by both the actions and services layer to communicate with third-party APIs.
   • Configuration and deployment artifacts (Docker, migration scripts) manage application start-up and environment setup.

3. Architectural Patterns and Principles
   • Separation of Concerns: The division among frontend (UI), backend controllers/handlers, business logic (actions), and persistence (models, SQL store) is clear.
   • Modular Design: Different packages and directories (middlewares, models, services, etc.) indicate that the design follows modularization, which supports scalability and easier maintenance.
   • Testability: Presence of test files for most components (e.g., actions_test.go, handlers_test.go) indicates an emphasis on testable code.
   • Integration with Continuous Integration/Deployment (CI/CD) tools is indicated through GitHub workflows and Docker configurations.
   
4. Relevant Technologies and Frameworks
   • Go (Golang) for backend development.
   • React (and TypeScript) for frontend development.
   • PostgreSQL (or similar relational database) for persistence.
   • Docker for containerization.
   • Various packages for logging, authentication (JWT), billing, email, and web utilities.

5. Guidelines for Tailoring the Diagram to Fider’s Specific Structure
   • Separate the diagram into clearly layered sections:
     - Client Layer: Mark the “public” folder and note that it uses React components, pages, and SSR.
     - Backend Layer: Indicate subcomponents for API handlers, business logic (actions), middleware, job processing, and models.
     - Database: Represent the persistent data store (diagram an “SQL Database” based on migration scripts).
     - External Services: Draw boxes for billing, email, OAuth providers, and webhooks.
     - DevOps/Deployment: Show Docker, GitHub CI/CD pipelines, and any orchestration tools.
   • Use directional arrows to highlight:
     - How requests flow from the frontend to the backend.
     - How the backend accesses the database and makes calls to external services.
     - How asynchronous jobs interact with core services (e.g., trigger a notification job after posting).
   • Color-code or use distinct shapes for:
     - UI components (e.g., rounded rectangles for frontend modules)
     - Backend services (e.g., standard rectangles)
     - External integrations (e.g., cloud icons or distinct colors)
     - Data stores (e.g., cylinder shape for databases)
   • Label each component and note key responsibilities. For instance, label “Actions” as the business logic layer handling critical operations like authentication, billing, and user management; label “Handlers” as the API endpoints that the client interacts with.
   • Emphasize interconnections by drawing dashed lines or directional arrows from API endpoints to middlewares, then to actions, models, and subsequently the database.
   • Don’t forget to include the asynchronous process flow (jobs/tasks) triggering from business events.

6. Final Instructions for the Diagram
   • Clearly label each component (e.g., “Frontend UI – React”, “API Handlers – Go”, “Business Logic (Actions)”, “Database – PostgreSQL”, “External Billing (Paddle)”, “External Email Providers”).
   • Use directional arrows to indicate data flow:
       – From the user’s browser (frontend) to the API Gateway (handlers)
       – From the API layer to business logic (actions) and middleware
       – From the business logic to the database and external services.
   • Apply color coding or different shapes: For example, use a specific color for client-side, another for server-side, and distinct icons for external services.
   • Ensure the diagram captures both synchronous flows (HTTP requests, API responses) and asynchronous processing (background jobs, tasks).
   • Include notes to explain which components correspond to key directories like “app”, “public”, “services”, and “migrations” to make it easier for someone acquainted with the file structure to quickly verify the diagram.

By following these steps, you will produce a comprehensive system design diagram that accurately captures Fider’s architecture—from its modern frontend built in React, through a robust Go backend with layered business logic and API handling, all the way to its integrations with external services and persistent data storage. This detailed diagram will be an invaluable resource for understanding both the high-level system interactions and the detailed internal structure of the application.
</explanation>
